### The movement's beats, in order, as they stand on the page

1. **CHAPTER 411, FRIDAY THE THIRD. THE BOOK, THE ROOM, THE HEAD-RULE, AND A PAPER ON THE DOOR.** A room over a joiner's shop at the top of Fish Street with a long table in it, four benches and a lamp on a nail, no board on the wall, no list, no name over the door, let out on a Sunday by a man of about thirty-four who carries a bowl down to the step at two and takes it in at six and does not ask who is going in. The book is bound in a re-backed canvas about two inches thick, was begun on the twentieth of April past, and carries **thirty heads on the said day**. Its head is five lines: four lines to be filled under every head, being what the thing is, where it came from, who stands where it is, and what it does not show; the refusals are on it and are not smaller than the rest; nothing entered in it is a decision and nothing binds anybody and a man's no goes in with the reason against his name and his name as plainly as a yes; head-notes are read out on a Sunday with the reader's name and the hour in his own hand on the day. **The second line of that head has been rubbed at the end for about forty years of an elbow on a table and the man who keeps the room declined to say why, because the first year is not this year and is not his telling.** Four people read the volume through from the first page to the last, being the holder of that writ, a woman of no office, a man of about forty-six who mends nets, and at about half past six a man of about twenty-six who stacks empties. A count of eleven people who cannot read was arrived at that day by two people counting separately and adding: **six by the woman of about fifty-eight in her own trade, five by the man of about twenty-six on the quay, and six and five is eleven.** The reader said out loud that on a Sunday he will read every head-note off that table and write his own name and the hour under each in his own hand on the day, and that he is a man of forty-six and does not charge a room for reading to a man who cannot read. And at the top left of that door there is a paper with four lines on it, under a drawing-pin and a fold of oiled paper, which is not the notice of the seventeenth of May past.
2. **CHAPTER 412, SATURDAY THE FOURTH. THE PAPER ON THE DOOR, IN FULL, AND THE MAN WHO PUT IT UP.** A lamp of about four inches was found burning in that room on the night of the nineteenth of August at eleven, and there was nothing in the room with it; on the days following eleven people of that harbor were asked one at a time whether they had been in that room on that night; **one of the eleven was**; the person who found the lamp will not say which and has been asked by two persons of that street to say and has not said; anybody found to have been in that room on that night is to take himself, or herself, off out of that harbor before the twentieth of September next. It went up on the thirty-first of August past at about eleven in the morning, before the market filled, and the man who put it up is **Walter Dunn, about forty-one, the night man at the fish market steps for eleven years**, who was on a ladder in the passage behind that shop at about eleven o'clock on the nineteenth with a shutter off his hand, and the top left pane of the fanlight over that passage door has been out since the spring. The room holds a table, two benches and a lamp on a nail and has no cupboard, no chest, no shelves and no box in it, so nothing of any size was put down and taken out again in four minutes. **He has the eleven written down in his own hand in his coat in the order he asked them in and has shown them to nobody and has not destroyed them, and has been asked twice to take the paper down and has not.** He said the whole of that paper is a date at the end of the fourth line, and a name on a door is a different kind of thing from a date on a door and cannot be taken off again.
3. **CHAPTER 413, SUNDAY THE FIFTH. THE FIRST LETTING, THE BOWL, THE READING, A REFUSAL ENTERED, AND ONE QUESTION AT THE END OF THE TABLE.** The bowl stood on the top stone of the step from two until six and whatever was in it was what the room took, and ninepence was in it at six o'clock. About twenty people went up and four came down and eleven of the twenty could not read and were not asked to prove it. The reader read the head-notes in the order they were in and wrote his own name and the hour under each. **The nineteenth head, entered on the ninth of June, is of two boats of a man of about forty-four of the second lay, of nine and eleven tons, who came on the seventh of June and said no, and it carries four lines and his name and an eleven-word reason, and it was read out in that room for the first time and he was not in it and was not asked to be.** At about half past three the woman of about fifty-eight stood up at her end of the table and refused out loud to have the figure of lamp oil entered, being four hundred and fifty pence with February's three hundred and seventy-eight above it and both dates on a board, and gave her reason that a figure read out in a room is a different kind of figure from a figure on a board and would be in about eleven markets by Tuesday, and **her no was entered in the same hand and the same size as every other line on the page with her name and the hour against it, as the thirty-first head, and was read out in that room, and she was not thanked in that room.** At about ten to four a woman of about sixty-one of the third lay came up those stairs one step at a time with a stick and asked one question at the end of that table: **does that book hold a thing a person made themselves.** She was told it does not. She said it is the wrong book for her and that she has been in the wrong book for about forty-two years, and that she has got one about eleven inches by eight in a box in her back room, that it has been in that box since the year she was nineteen, that she has not looked at it in a long while, and that she would like to look at it in a room with people in it because she has had forty-two years of nobody. She was told the room was open at one o'clock on a Sunday, that anybody who brought a thing to that table could take it away again, and that about twenty people would be in the room. She said twenty. **Nobody thanked her and there is no name against her and there is not going to be one.**
4. **CHAPTER 414, MONDAY THE SIXTH. THE WIPE, THE CISTERN, A CAULKER'S DAY, AND A ROOM IN JUNE.** The seventieth wipe and the seventy-ninth cistern charge, walked on by none of it, the top name on the rota board still off it. A caulker of about twenty-three asked for that day by name on the Friday and paid in coin on the flat of the bench stone at about four. A man of about thirty-four with the keys to two stores took the holder of that writ up a passage to shelf four, and **a panel of worked glass about eleven inches by eight was looked at standing up and was not taken out of its box, and there is a person in it about four inches high with a shoulder and a hip and a hand standing a little way inside a door.** A note of four lines has been pinned to that lid since the fourth of June, signed with a name and not an office, saying the glass is sound at the join, that the join will take a mend and it will take a backing, and where it came from. **The holder of that writ said out loud that he has been in this harbor nine months and can look in about nine hundred places where something is kept and can stand there and say a person is in that panel, and the book on the table over the joiner's shop says in four lines what every one of those places does not show and does not say this one, and that that is not a lie in it: a dash is not a lie, a dash is a hole.** He said nobody is to be charged for that panel, that nobody is going to be told they have to move it, and that the man who put it in a box will not be asked about it. **Ned Vaile, about fifty-five, who marks at the fish quay and keeps the marks of that volume and is not paid for it, said that on the eighteenth of June past there were four men in that room, two of them off boats, that he copied the note into the first line and put the shelf in against the third, that he asked one of those four men in front of the other three what that panel was not fit for, and was told he did not know, and that none of the other three said anything, and that he put a dash because he was not going to write down a thing nobody had said to him. He said a dash is true and a dash is a hole and that he has known it was a hole since the eighteenth of June and has not come back to it in eighty days, and that he has never once gone down that volume with a pencil and counted what was in the fourth line of each head, and that a man who has not looked does not get to tell a man who has looked what is there.**
5. **CHAPTER 415, TUESDAY THE SEVENTH. THE FORTY-SIXTH WAGE TUESDAY, AND A REFUSAL TO READ A DOOR NOTICE ALOUD.** The column has twenty-six lines and one hundred and four marks and twenty envelopes in a chest and has not moved since the fourth of April past, and forty-five weeks stood fallen due at the open of these ten days and forty-six stand at the close of them, and the forty-seventh falls on Tuesday the fourteenth of September next. **A man of about thirty-four asked the man of about forty-six to read the four lines off that door out loud in that room on a Sunday, to everybody in it, and was refused in his own mouth with his own reason, being that those eleven would never hear a head-note in that room again if they were sitting at that table waiting for the paper, and being that he had been on the wrong side of a paper he could not read at nine years old in that harbor, with his mother reading it to him out loud in a kitchen, and had thirty-seven years of not knowing whether she had made any of it up, and said that was a selfish reason and he had not got a better one. He said that on the Wednesday he was going to tell eleven people one at a time in daylight and face to face that there was a paper on that door, and that he was not going to read it to them, and that they were not to ask him.** He priced the Sunday off his own slate: two hours and twenty minutes, a shilling not earned, and a bowl on a step that has to be made whether he is there or not, and said there is no figure in that harbor for what a man gives up on a Sunday because he is reading a book for people who cannot read, and that is why it goes in the second column.
6. **CHAPTER 416, WEDNESDAY THE EIGHTH. THE ELEVEN TOLD, ONE AT A TIME, IN DAYLIGHT, AND A MAN COMING TO HIS OWN PAPER.** Forty-four pence went out for a loaf and a half, a candle and a pot, to a man of about thirty-eight with a boat of about thirteen tons and no papers who was out all day on the sixth clause of a notice in a different street. **The man of about forty-six walked on his own two feet from about nine in the morning to about four in the afternoon and had eleven conversations with eleven people, in the street and in their own doors, and told each of them that there is a paper with four lines on it at the top left of that door, that it went up on the thirty-first of August, that a volume is read out loud at that table on a Sunday at two o'clock, that there is a bowl on the step and they may put a penny in it or not, and that the notice on the wall in the other street is a different paper on a different wall — and showed none of them the paper, read it to none of them, and told one of them that he had not read it himself and was not going to. Four of the eleven went on longer than a minute and the shortest was about forty seconds, and not one of the eleven asked him to read it.** The eleventh was a man of about sixty-two who has sat on the same bollard at the head of a slip since June, who said it was the first anybody had told him about anything in that harbor in about a month and that he would come on Sunday if the door were not shut. **Tom Barlas, who is the man of about thirty-four who lets that room out, came up the stairs at about four and asked whether anybody had answered the paper and was told no, and Walter Dunn, the man of about forty-one who put that paper up, had come up the same stairs at about half past two, before him, and been told the same answer, and he was then told the same thing and not before, because that man had put it up and had been carrying it for eight days, and that two people in that harbor had been in that room on Sundays and had gone away and told nobody, and that a man who has been twice to a room and told nobody is not in a position to go into a taproom and say a paper on a door is a lie, and he went down the stairs and did not say one word.** A caulker of about twenty-three was asked for Friday the tenth by name at about five and said he would want it said to him on the Thursday. A woman of no office put forty pence of her own into the bowl on the step at a quarter past one, out of her own hand, and did not say why and was not asked.
7. **CHAPTER 417, THURSDAY THE NINTH. THE EIGHTIETH CISTERN, ONE QUESTION ASKED ONCE, AND A PENCIL PUT DOWN.** The cistern was charged and walked on at about half past nine, being the eightieth time, the rota being a Monday and a Thursday, and the top name on that board is still off it. **The man of about forty-six walked down to the third lay at about two in the afternoon and asked a woman of about sixty-one one question, being whether she would bring a thing out of a box in her back room to that table on Sunday the twelfth at one o'clock and look at it with about twenty people in the room, and offered her a barrow and a hand at the top of two flights of stairs at half past twelve, and did not offer again. She asked him one question back, being whether there would be people in the room when she looked at it, and was told that there would be about twenty. She said she would be there at one o'clock and not before and that she is not going early to be helped in and that she is not going to be thanked at the top of that stair or the bottom of it or anywhere else, and that if anybody in that room says a kind thing to her she will walk out, and he said he would tell them so and would not soften it because a thing that is softened in a message is a thing that has been said twice. No second question was asked her by anybody in that yard on the said day.** Her room is nine marks a year and has been for eleven years and the rope walk in the back of it does not run. And in that shed at about six in the evening the holder of that writ said out loud that **he was not going to count a public volume with a pencil in his own hand**, and gave the reason, being that a man with a stake is not a count and is a complaint with a number at the end of it, and that a man of about fifty-three with a bad back who counted a municipal return on his own time in five afternoons was a different thing; and that he would not stand in a street and ask a man to come and read that volume, and that if nobody comes then nobody comes; **and he put the pencil down on the bench stone two inches from that yard's own leaf and left it there.**
8. **CHAPTER 418, FRIDAY THE TENTH. NONE UNDER A FIGURE THAT CANNOT BE TAKEN OFF.** A day at a berth came in and a second caulker's day went out at the same figure and the bag did not move up. **There has been no barrel of lamp oil in that harbor since the twenty-ninth day of August and there was none on the said day, and a board at an end stall carries four hundred and fifty pence with February's three hundred and seventy-eight standing visible above it and both dates on the board, and the figure of the first of June was not taken off and cannot be taken off.** A man of about thirty-three put a tin can on that board and was told there is none. The woman of about fifty-eight wrote one word in chalk on the edge of that board in her own hand, where she wrote it in August, **and would not rule a line under the oil figure**, and gave her reason, being that a line with one word on it under a figure goes up the street in about an hour and that by the end of next month men will be saying the oil was never here. There is no flour in that market and none is coming this month and physic is at fourteen pence with none in that harbor and the mole-head light is out and its lens has been out since the seventh of May past. **A man of about thirty-one of that lay with a chart in a bag stood at the end of that table for ten minutes and said one sentence at the bottom of those stairs, being that somebody is going to read that volume out loud and about eleven people who cannot read are going to be told it on somebody's word, and that in about a fortnight one of the eleven will say in a market that a thing in that book is not so and that no arrangement stops that — and is not on a sheet and is not on a list and nobody in that yard is to go and ask him about a chart in a bag.** A caulker of about twenty-three was paid for the sixth time since the tenth of August, and the six are the seventeenth, the twenty-first, the twenty-seventh and the thirty-first of August past and the sixth and the tenth of September, and the tenth of August past was the payment before those six and is not one of them, and he said out loud that the holder of that writ was going to have him on the Monday, and was told that he is not on the Monday until he is asked for it by name on the Friday before, and that there is no board with a name on it in that yard and there is not going to be one, and said that he will not be in that room on Sunday and did not say why and was not asked.
9. **CHAPTER 419, SATURDAY THE ELEVENTH. THE ROOM GOT READY, AND A MAN WITH A PENCIL COMES UP A STAIR.** The joiner's room with the joiner at the bottom of the stair and the volume lying at the end of a table he glues battens along from six in the morning. A man of about forty-six cleaned the table with a scraper and a bucket because it is a table, brought the four benches out from under the wall, found the lamp on a nail and did not light it, and brought a barrow up two flights of stairs at about half past twelve and stood it at the top. **Tom Barlas put the bowl on the step at two and carried it in at six and it was empty, and said that he has never written one of the people who came up that stair down, because a list in a room anybody can pay half a penny to walk into is a list of everybody in that harbor who could not afford half a penny.** The reader said he would read twenty-two of the thirty-one heads on the Sunday and would not read the other nine, being six pieces of glass off three wrecks together with a lamp, a door plate and a box of tally sticks. And at about half past four, because the door was off the latch, **a man of about thirty-one called Arthur Sennett, who writes figures on a slate for a buyer at a fish stall and has done for nine years, came up that stair and read the whole of that volume from the back to the front and then from the front to the back for about fifty minutes and wrote nothing and asked nobody anything and shut it and squared it to the edge of that table and went down the stairs and out into Fish Street, and nobody in that yard knew he had been in the room until the following afternoon, and nobody in that yard sent for him or spoke to him or knew he was coming.**
10. **CHAPTER 420, SUNDAY THE TWELFTH. THE PANEL, THE ROOM THAT EMPTIED, THE BOX, THE BOOK, THE PENCIL, AND THE READ-BACK.** The barray went to the top of the stairs at half past twelve. **She came up at one o'clock, cut the rope with a short knife, took the thing out with both hands, set it down on the long table and stood looking at it, and then stepped back from the table so that the people coming up could see it, and went and stood at the back of that room against the wall with her stick in front of her, and did not look at it again for the rest of that afternoon.** It is about eleven inches by eight with a plain mitred deal frame and a nail in each corner, and there is a face in it and the face is about four inches high and is turned away from the room, and what is in the face is a room with a door in it, the door shut, a figure a little way inside it with its back to whoever is looking, the hand up at the height of its own chest with the fingers not shut, and light coming in on the side of the room the door is not on. She said she was not going to say anything about it and that if anybody said a kind thing she would walk out. About twenty people went up and four came down. **The reader read twenty-two head-notes, the first at about two minutes past two and the last at about twenty-six minutes past three, and the last was the woman of about fifty-eight's refusal, and she said from the middle of the room that it is a strange thing to hear your own no read out in a room and she would not have had it any other way and is not going to say a kind thing about it now or ever. He shut the volume and squared it to the edge of the table, and the pencil went behind his ear, and that is how it stood when the room emptied.** The room emptied at about ten to five without a sound anybody in that street heard. She put the lid on, cut the rope, and went down, and the first flight backwards with the barrow's wheel against the step, and the man of about forty-six took the other end without being asked and without saying anything, and **said nothing at the top of that stair and nothing at the bottom of it, and nobody in that room or on that step said one kind word to her, and nobody in that harbor has said one kind word to her since.** A man of about forty-one came down the slip at ten past five and said that he had not been looking at the thing on the table, that he was looking at the door the whole time, that he got to the bottom of those stairs and could not tell in which order he had come down them, and that he had to go back up and put his hand on the frame to find out; and that he has had a cold in his teeth since about three o'clock and a taste of iron like a nail and it is not a fever and he could go out and lift a barrow of shavings; and that he knows the number of his son's fingers; and that he is not going to be a man in that harbor who goes round saying it. **The holder of that writ had been outside in Fish Street since a quarter past four and did not go in, and said he had nothing to give him, and said that if he wants to know what is on that table he can go and ask the woman of about sixty-one and she will tell him no.** At about ten past five, on his way out, **Arthur Sennett asked for the volume, sat on the bench at the joiner's end, and counted the heads on the back of his own left hand with the stub of pencil behind his ear and said: thirty-one heads; thirty of them have four lines under the head; one has three; and the head of it at the front says four lines under every head and says in its second line that the refusals are on it too and are not smaller than the rest; and it is the twenty-second, and its third line ends in a dash. He wrote it in four lines in pencil on the inside of the back cover with his own name and the date, and said that he was not in that room on the eighteenth of June and is not going to say who was, and that four people stood in that room while he said it and not one of the four put the question to him.** The holder of that writ asked one thing in the passage, in about six words, and Ned Vaile said it was true, and the holder of that writ said that he had read that head on Friday the third and put his thumb on the third line and left the volume shut on that table and had not counted anything, and **then neither of them said one word about it, and they went down the hill together and neither of them said one word about it.**

## Where the story is at the end of Chapter 410

### The movement's beats, in order, as they stand on the page

1. **CHAPTER 401, TUESDAY THE TWENTY-FOURTH, THE FORTY-FOURTH WAGE TUESDAY. THE KNOCK.** He went up the hill at twenty to ten with his hands empty and knocked on a shut door in a corridor where, on the evening of Monday the twenty-third of August, he had stood and read nine lines twice and had not knocked. The door was opened by Saul Drury, a copying clerk of that office, about forty, who said nothing and left the door standing open. The hour ran from ten until about twenty to eleven, and the clerk was in the room the whole of it and put a lamp on a table without being asked and stood six feet off and said the hour in five words. The thing on the far shelf is about nine inches by six and its edge over nine inches is cut and not broken and the arris is still on it. It has a seam across it at about a third of the way up. **THE HOLDER SAID THAT A SEAM IS WHERE ONE MAKER'S PRESSURE MET ANOTHER'S AND NEITHER WON ALL THE WAY, AND THAT IT IS THE ONLY HONEST MARK IN RECOVERED WORK, AND THAT IT SAYS TWO PEOPLE MADE IT AND BOTH OF THEM WERE FRIGHTENED, AND THAT HE CANNOT SAY WHICH OF THE TWO WAS IN THE ROOM IT WAS CUT IN.** The woman of no office said that was not an answer; he said it was the only one he had. It went back on the far shelf on the same place under the same number. **The middle shelf was between the door and the far wall on the way in and on the way out and the holder did not turn his head at it or at the claim book above it and the clerk did not turn his either.** A request for another hour of the same thing was made in the corridor at about ten past eleven and refused in a clerk's nine words.
2. **THE AFTERTASTE, AND IT IS A REAL THING AND NOT A DISEASE.** The holder came out of the room with a window at about the height of his head, a board across the outside of it, a line of daylight under the board that does not move, water about four feet down going the other way and a man's hand on it going fast and **not frightened**. The woman of no office came out with a smell of tar and a hot iron and something under it she has no name for, and a woman counting in the dark and not losing her place and going to the end anyway. **They have the hand and the counting and neither of them can put them together, and on Sunday the twenty-ninth they agreed in their own mouths to stop and not to try to match them, because the day one of them matches them by guessing is the day one of them is wrong for the rest of their lives.** That agreement is the whole of what the aftertaste does to the plot in this movement and it is not a disease and not a fever and not glass and it is told out of two bodies and not out of a paper.
3. **CHAPTER 402, WEDNESDAY THE TWENTY-FOURTH'S NEXT DAY. THE REFUSAL ON THE DOOR, IN THE CLERK'S HAND.** Four lines, no seal, no office, the clerk's own name and the word *clerk* after it, and it says a second paper will be on that door on the second of September and not on any day before it. The holder identified the hand from a line the same man had ruled with a flat rule at about ten past ten on the Tuesday. The woman of no office did not go up the hill again and said on the mole that the thing she is carrying is not sitting still and that she would not say the other half of it.
4. **CHAPTERS 403 TO 409. THE RETURN, AND THE COUNT, AND THE MAN WHO COUNTED IT.** A sheet about two foot by three is nailed to nine feet of wall inside the door of the office on the west basin. It is the return of recovered glass entered at that harbor since the first of April, ruled in five blocks by month, with a line for every day and a figure in the right-hand column on a day a thing came in and a single stroke across the line on a day nothing did, and a space two inches deep at the foot with the word *carried* over it and nothing in it. Five small figures in the hand of a clerk of about sixty stand at the head of the five blocks and are the number of lines in each block that carry a figure. **A man of about fifty-three with a bad back, Peat Marrow, who works a winch on the third lay, counted the five blocks on five afternoons, one at a time, with a stub of pencil on the flat of his own left hand, on his own time, and was not paid for it and was not thanked for it and said it once in a front street on a day he had named in advance.** The count: **one hundred and forty-five lines, one hundred and sixteen carrying a figure, twenty-nine struck across, and the summands seventy-one, ninety-six, seventy-nine, eighty-eight and fifty-seven, which is three hundred and ninety-one.** He counted the lines of the first and second blocks twice and the other three once and added each of the hundred and sixteen figures exactly once, and gave the reason for not going over the figures again, which is that he was not going to start wanting it to be a different number. On the first of September the figure went into the first column of that yard's own leaf in the holder's hand with the five summands and the line count under it and no name against it, and was read out in that shed at about ten past four with the hour against it.
5. **CHAPTERS 403 TO 409. THE YARD'S MONEY, AND THE MAN OF FIFTY-EIGHT'S SLATE.** Three days at a berth came in and two days of a caulker and a loaf and a half and a candle and a pot went out, and the bag stands at two hundred and eighty-four pence. A woman of about fifty-eight put her slate on the bench stone face up on the Friday and said that six men asked her what it costs to be in a boat of that yard's for a day and that one of them, who is fifty-one and has a boat called the *Anna Ray* of about fifty tons and is owed nineteen winters, said he would not do it for that, and that she said good to him. On the Saturday a man of about forty-four with a shop on the far street asked in the middle aisle of that market how many pieces of recovered glass have been landed and entered at that harbor, and was told that there was not a figure, and that if there was one it was not going on anything and not going in that front street and not going on the wall in that other street.
6. **CHAPTER 405, SATURDAY THE TWENTY-EIGHTH. THE REASON, ENTERED ONCE.** In that shed, in the yard's own mouth: the yard's time went into the first column and into a convoy and into a caulker's day; the fourth column is a page no man can check; and there was a man on the flat of the bench stone at four in the morning on the Friday who had to be paid first and was paid before anybody in that yard put a word down about what a thing is not. **THE FOURTH COLUMN THEREFORE TOOK NO LINE IN ANY OF THESE TEN DAYS AND THERE IS NO HUNDRED AND TWENTY-SIXTH LINE IN IT AND THE COLUMN IS NOT CLOSED AND IS NOT A STRIKE-OUT AND NOBODY HAS CLOSED IT.** Every later ledger carries the fact that the reason has been entered and does not enter it again.
7. **CHAPTERS 406 TO 409. THE PEOPLE, EACH ON A PAGE AND ON A DAY.** Isaac Fell, a caulker of about twenty-three, asked for by name on the Wednesday for the Friday and on the Saturday for the Tuesday, and paid in coin on the flat of the bench stone at about four in the afternoon at one hundred and sixty-eight pence out of that yard's own figures, twice, neither time thanked, and he said that the nineteenth and the twentieth days of August past are not in the bag and are not going in. A copyist of about fifty-nine, twenty-two years in a room off that market, who has never once asked what she is copying and gave the reason, being that a copyist who stops copying is a copyist who has admitted she copied something, and who sold him one sheet for a penny out of his own hand. A clerk of about sixty who has been in that room twenty-two years, is owed a quarter of a pound, has no book and no power, and said that he would not have thought that one was right. A man of about fifty with two papers on one table who told him the register copy of what this yard gave on the seventh of July is on a shelf behind that counter and has not been asked for in fifty-five days, and who has read a nine-line sheet four times and has not answered it and said the answer to a thing like that is a piece of paper with a name at the foot of it and not a word. A man of about thirty-one of the third lay with a chart in a bag who said that somebody would say the page was blank and not say why, and was told yes. A man of about thirty-eight with a boat of about thirteen tons and no papers on her who has been out on the sixth clause twice in six weeks on his own account and said so out loud on the second lay and asked for nothing. A man of about fifty-one on the crown of that mole with his page and his stone and no figure and **fifty days of silence and nothing given to him by anybody.**
8. **CHAPTER 410, THURSDAY THE SECOND OF SEPTEMBER. THE SECOND PAPER, AND THE FIGURE AT THE FOOT OF IT.** The refusal was taken down by the hand that wrote it and a second paper was pinned under the first at the same corner, carrying the same three lines naming two as permitted and one as present for the whole of the hour and the same three lines under them. **The hour is ten in the morning on the fifth day of October, being a Tuesday, at that door.** At the foot of it, where the first had a seal line, there are five lines in the clerk's own hand and no seal, and the reason the paper was held nine days is a figure, and the figure is seven: a copy of that thing, marked with where it came from, is seven hours at that bench and a pair of hands, and one hour is one, and both of those are true and neither of them cancels the other. **The holder read those five lines five times, did not knock, did not touch the door and went back down the hill. The room is entered once in these ten days and the second time in this volume is not this one's.**
9. **THE READ-BACK AT TEN PAST FIVE, ON THE FLAT OF THE BENCH STONE, WITH THE LIGHT NOT LIT.** The ship's hand read the leaf back in full in her own left hand, all four columns including the empty one, with both definitions of the four figures on the face of the reading, and stated that the fourth column has one hundred and twenty-five lines in it at the hour and one hundred and twenty-five at the close and has taken no line since the twenty-third of August, and that that is not a closure and not a strike-out.

### The four figures at the close of Chapter 410, and which definition each is

- **AT THE HOUR OF THE READING: ONE HUNDRED AND FORTY-TWO / FIVE HUNDRED AND EIGHTY-SEVEN / NONE / ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIVE. AT THE CLOSE OF THE DAY: ONE HUNDRED AND FORTY-THREE / FIVE HUNDRED AND EIGHTY-NINE / NONE / ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIVE.**
- **THE FIRST COLUMN'S FIGURE IS A COUNT OF ENTRIES AND THE FOURTH'S IS A COUNT OF LINES, AND A DAY OF THE FIRST COLUMN CARRIES ONE ENTRY AGAINST IT WHATEVER ELSE THAT DAY PRINTED, SO THAT A STRANGER WITH A LEAF AND A PENCIL CAN COUNT BOTH. THE SECOND COLUMN'S FIGURE IS THAT LEDGER'S OWN AND IS NOT A COUNT OF ANYTHING A STRANGER CAN CHECK FROM A MOLE.** Both definitions are on the face of Chapter 410's own reading, in the ship's mouth, and the ten-day run is re-derived from the close of Chapter 400: the first column's base is one hundred and thirty-three and takes one entry against each of the ten days with no day in two of them; the second column's base is five hundred and thirty-nine and takes five a day, three before the hour of that day's reading and two after it; the third takes none and nobody is appointed to it; **the fourth takes no line in this volume and stands where it stands.**
- **THE COUNT IS THE FOURTH THING ON THE FACE OF THIS MOVEMENT AND IT IS NOT ONE OF THE FOUR.** Three hundred and ninety-one, pieces of recovered glass landed and entered at that harbor since the first of April, off a municipal return, counted one line at a time with a pencil by a man on his own time, with five summands and a line count written under it so a stranger can take it again, and with no name against it and in no mouth.

### What is owed and what is not

**OWED TO THE BOOK BY A LATER MOVEMENT OF THIS VOLUME AND NOT BY THIS BATCH:** the fourth column's reason has been entered once and every later ledger carries the fact and enters it again nowhere; the second paper's hour is the fifth day of October, being a Tuesday, at ten in the morning, at that door, and the second entry into that room in this volume is the climax's and is not this batch's; **SOMETHING IS TO GO INTO THAT FOURTH BOX IN THIS VOLUME AGAINST THE WISH OF THE MAN OF ABOUT FIFTY AND NOBODY IN THAT YARD IS TO ASK HIM ABOUT IT**; the partial confession of a man of sixty-one is this volume's and comes down to the shed in four sentences and is not in these ten chapters; the far bench keeps its one shoe; the twelve-term sweep must be run again by the phase that writes the next batch and by the volume close; and the day-counts below run on one a day and nothing turns on a round figure.

**NOT OWED AND NOT TO BE RESTARTED:** the hundred and twenty-sixth line in that ledger, which nobody is to enter in this volume; a hundred and seventy-first day of the ninety; a forty-sixth wage Tuesday paid; a second loss of flour; the third of the three things in that room and the claim on it, which is not withdrawn and which nobody is going to ask to have withdrawn; the name of the office at the foot of that first paper's seal line out loud, which is Movement 5's and is said once by a working man reading the foot of a paper out loud in a room; the title of the charter, which is in no mouth before the last movement; the bellwright of that harbor, who is not asked; Sera Mott, who is not asked again; the plate at the fifth seam, in eleven feet, with its note open, not looked at, not measured, not touched, not asked about and not named; and the first echo's witness, who stays where he is.

### The eleven elements the volume declared, each with its count and its ruling, off the face of the fifty chapters

1. **THE CENTRAL PRESSURE — RULED PAID, IN FULL.** One sealed instrument with two seals and one signature, four prices, of which the fourth is a statement and is not a thing; eleven leaves in six hands in four places; eleven people holding them asked on one day, nine said no in nine words of their own, one did not say yes and did not say no, one said no down a coast road on the Monday, giving **ten noes and one that was neither**, and one of the ten carries a reason that is about a line of writing and not about a person. A name and an hour on all thirteen lines of a sheet and a price and a payer on eleven, and the price on all eleven is the word *nothing*. A tender of about ninety tons at the outer water. A page of six names and a boat and no figure on a mole. **And this yard charged nobody for the writing and wrote to none of the five towns that hold the copies and did not ask who put the page up on the wall.**
2. **THE STARTING STATE — ALL TEN ITEMS AUDITED, AND ALL TEN ARE STILL STANDING AND NOT ONE IS IMPROVED.** A bag with nothing in it; a harbor poorer than on the fourteenth of May; a notice of eight clauses on a market wall for ninety-eight days, untouched; a page of forty lines on a wall four days up that coast; the Storm-Reader stage taken once and the mark's new use closed at four figures with no fifth and two nine-mark seasons unpaid; a wreck of about nineteen tons and six owners ashore with no boat and a man of about fifty-one with a page on a mole and no figure; a custody room with three items under three numbers and none returned and none asked for; the three figures that must not be swapped, in that order; about eleven people who cannot read the notice; and a day lost on Thursday the first of July to a thing that has no name in it. **A CLOSE THAT FOUND ANY ONE OF THEM IMPROVED WOULD BE WRONG. THIS ONE DOES NOT FIND ANY IMPROVED.**
3. **THE STARTING RELATIONSHIPS — ALL EIGHT RULED PAID, AND LOCK L18 RULED SPECIFICALLY.** Calder and Mara, and the apology owed and not said in Movement 1 and paid once in Movement 2 on the water on the twenty-first of July, not forgiven, not thanked, and a procedure asked for instead, and the committed relationship begun once on a mole at about six on the twenty-second and not sealed and not a marriage and forty marks first after food neither reduced nor paid. Calder and Nessa, and the last page of the volume read by her and not by him. Calder and Alden, and the count is three and all three are the lock's own disambiguation, and there is no fragment, no report talk, no second story and no confession in any of the fifty chapters and the yard enters on all fifty that he was not approached and that neither brother went near the other. Calder and Bevin, off the stone, forty marks whole, the three nots standing unasked for a sixth week, the third column unfilled and unappointed, his surname on no page. Calder and Tobias Wren, sixty-one in all fifty chapters, eleven pieces of a boat whose age is unstated on every page, one sentence in the whole volume and it is on the face of Chapter 385, not sent for, not asked, not thanked, not a teacher, not a door, not a sacrifice. And the wardrobe, every man and woman on a page and none of them a witness, a symbol, an officer, a member of anything, a courier or a face.
4. **THE STARTING POWER LEVEL — RULED VERIFIED ON ALL SIX COUNTS, ALL OF THEM ZERO.** No stage taken in any of the fifty chapters. The Faultreader stage not re-taken. The Bellwright stage not improved. The Storm-Reader stage not taken again. The word *keelwright* in no mouth, count zero. No echo entered, no vessel entered, no practice trace surfaced. And the condition named nowhere, and paying its cost is not naming it. **What he did instead of taking anything: he asked about eleven masters one at a time, carried a sheet with about thirty men's names on it into company, read a shape out loud in a boat, stopped a squadron's work on a reach with his own mouth, said what it cost out loud once on a mole, and walked away from a man with a form in his hand without asking him a single question.**
5. **THE FOUR MAJOR LOCATIONS AND THE THREE FORUMS — RULED PAID, WITH THREE COUNTS ON THE FORUMS.** The outer water and Ternwatch; Veyr's diplomatic quarter; border reefs and a convoy of confiscated memory vessels; and the harbor line, the market wall, the shed and the mole, which never leave the page. **The harbor authority's hearing room is named on no page of the fifty chapters and the count is zero, and what stands in its place is the reeve's office on the west basin, which lists, enters and pays a day with a boat and two men out of a berth fund, and whose list is not a schedule and binds nobody, and which decides no contested claim in this volume. The Morrow circuit office decides provenance and custody and is named in five chapters and holds three things and a claim and a paper on a door. The Court of Wreck Claims is on no page of the fifty chapters and the count of the phrase is zero, and an institution that is on no page cannot speak.**
6. **THE MAJOR FACTIONS AS A SYSTEM AND NOT AS VILLAINS — RULED PAID ON ALL SEVEN, NONE A VILLAIN.** A Crown that is an instrument, a standing instruction, a patrol, a printed nine-line claim, an inquiry that is an institution and does not speak, and a seal line. A Registry that is a seal and a countersignature and a word at the head of a form. A navy with internal disagreement in it, whose face on the page is a working man of nineteen at a tiller. About eleven masters asked one at a time in the same words, seven yes and four no with a reason each, the cost of the four being a man's day and not a figure. And about eleven people who cannot read the notice, a count of people arrived at by two people counting separately and adding, not a constituency, not named, nobody sent.
7. **THE FIVE MOVEMENTS, EACH PAID, IN ORDER — RULED PAID IN ALL FIVE, AND MOVEMENT 5 PAID IN THE OUTLINE'S OWN FOUR-PART ORDER: THE CONVOY, THE PATROL, HIM STOPPING THE NAVAL ACTION RATHER THAN CHASING THE EVIDENCE, AND THE ADMISSION.** All four are on the page and none is softened.
8. **THE VOLUME'S CLIMAX AND ITS FOUR ELEMENTS — RULED PAID IN ALL FOUR, AND THE ORDER OF THE REVEAL RULED SEPARATELY AND RULED FIXED.** The eleven weeks were read out in a public room over the fish market in the order they were signed, ten of them a week apart and the last twelve days after the one before it, no date moved to make it come out even, and the countersigned form's shape was read out **after** them and not before, and the reason was given out loud. And what was read aloud was the shape and not the sheet: the word *unsealed*, two ruled columns, the same eleven marks against the same eleven dates, two impressions he read neither, and the fourteenth of February cut into the timber. **He does not have the form, he has no copy of it, and no document of anybody's changes hands in that harbor on any of the fifty days.**
9. **THE CONCRETE RESOLUTION'S FOUR ITEMS, NONE OF THEM SOFT, THE THIRD ONE THE CROWN'S WIN — RULED PAID IN ALL FOUR.** Soren Vey loses his flagship and his command and is not in a room and his name is on the face of one instrument in Movement 1 and in no mouth, in no room, on no mole and in no market for the remaining forty-nine chapters. The Crown turns the defeat into a printed claim that independent salvagers are dangerous, and it is the nine-line sheet in the front street since the fourteenth of August, and it is true enough on the face of it that nobody who reads it can go up the street and say it is a lie, and **it is answered by nobody.** The inquiry's terms give two named people a supervised and limited look at one of three things behind a door, on a paper that names two as permitted and one as present, with a figure that is a time and a place and an arrival and is the only figure in the fifty chapters that is not a price anybody paid, and **the room is not entered, no digit of any of the three numbers is on any page, the third is not on the paper, the municipal claim on the third is not withdrawn, and no request for it has been made by anybody.** And a new seal line at the last page names a new office, in no mouth, with no minister in a room and nobody in a room.
10. **THE NEW-VOLUME QUESTION, ASKED ONCE AND ANSWERED NOWHERE — RULED PAID AND RULED UNANSWERED.** *If the Navy cannot own the sea by force, is the Crown going to try to own history by making it legally singular?* Asked once, out loud, by a man with no office, in the office on the west basin, at about ten to six on Sunday the twenty-second, in a room with a clerk of about sixty in it, naming no person. The clerk's whole answer is that he has not got a book for it. **No character answers it, nobody proposes anything in answer to it, nobody names a central body, a committee, an assembly, a fleet, a wing or a guard, and the count of the six categories printed as an enumeration anywhere in the fifty chapters is zero. No character says the word *singular* of a person, and the count of the word across the fifty chapters is one, being the question itself. It is not answered by the form, not answered by the seal line, not answered by the nine-line sheet and not answered by anything else in the fifty chapters.**
11. **THE PLANNED RELATIONSHIP AND POWER CHANGE — RULED PAID IN ALL THREE PARTS.** The coordinated-repair work paid as a beginning in Movement 4 and not as a stage, with a wage and a day and a person who is there on a Tuesday and a fifth thing that is a person and is not on a list. The apology paid once in Movement 2 and not forgiven and not thanked. And the committed relationship begun once on the crown of that mole at about six on the twenty-second of August, in a few sentences, not a marriage, not sealed, the work not merged, she not restored, and forty marks first after food neither reduced nor paid at the last page.

### The twelve prohibitions, counted one at a time, and the four that bite ruled in words

1. The Volume 07 question not answered and no central body, committee, assembly, fleet, wing or guard named — **the count of the six categories printed as an enumeration is ZERO and the count of *network* in a mouth is ZERO. HELD.**
2. No man in a room who is only ever a name, a seal or an office — **Ilya Serr in no room, Halven Rook on no page, the man in a coat of an office unnamed. HELD.**
3. No blackmail, no kidnapping, no fire, no personal threat to Mara — **the count of each is zero; the offer is an instrument and the refusal is honest. HELD.**
4. **IT MAY NOT IMPROVE THE HARBOUR'S POVERTY. RULED HELD AND RULED IN WORDS: the light is out and its lens has been out since the seventh of May, and the last figure anybody in that harbor has for a barrel of lamp oil is four hundred and fifty pence against February's three hundred and seventy-eight, and that figure has not come back down, and nobody in that front street said a figure of oil out loud in the whole volume. There is no flour in that market and none is coming this month. The north berth is out, the hose is dead until the spring, the tide gang is four men short, the third lay is one berth short and has been for four months, a cistern was charged fifteen times in fifty days and walked on every one of them, the hard at Ashtide is unanswered since the ninth of November, and nineteen winters stand disputed and unpaid. A harbor that lost half a transport's flour on the twenty-first of August is poorer for it.**
5. The forty-line page wins nothing by itself — **nothing on it won anything. HELD.**
6. The Gannet manifest not resolved, the compartment not named, three Gannet documents not made into four — **the count of each breach is zero. HELD.**
7. The custody room not entered and no digit of any of its three numbers named — **the room is entered on no page and the count of digits is zero. HELD.**
8. The seven standing debts not paid — **each stands at its full figure and none is paid, advanced, reduced or improved on any of the fifty days. HELD.**
9. No stage in Movements 1, 2, 3 or 4 — **the count is zero in each and zero in Movement 5. HELD.**
10. No sympathetic character lost to prove growth — **no character dies in any of the fifty chapters, no body is named and no casualty figure is printed; the one loss of flesh is two fingers off a left hand on the twelfth of July, paid out of his own hand, with a bonesetter who refused the work. HELD.**
11. **IT MAY NOT USE THE WORD *CROWN* AS A THING CALDER TAKES, NOR LET HIM ACCEPT ANY AUTHORITY, TITLE OR SOLE COMMAND. RULED HELD AND RULED IN WORDS: he is a holder of a writ with no office behind him and no instrument and no power; he refuses to answer an instrument in a shed, refuses to put a man's name on a list, refuses to take a company out on a flood without a person asked for that day by name, and says out loud in a room that he is not able to hand any of it over and is not able to answer for anybody; and when the squadron's work stopped on that reach it stopped because thirty men heard a word at the same minute from one mouth and not because he gave an order. The count of any office, title, command, authority or allegiance accepted by him across the fifty chapters is zero.**
12. **IT MAY NOT END IN A VICTORY THAT IMPROVES A PRICE LIST. RULED HELD AND RULED IN WORDS: the volume ends with a bag of one mark, a mole-head light out, a custody-room door with a paper on it that gives two people a supervised look at one thing and not a taking, a nine-line sheet nobody has answered, a sheet with thirty men's names on it in a master's pocket that is not in this harbor, a market with no flour in it, and a fourth column whose hundred and twenty-fifth line is the last line in that book and the column is not closed. Not one figure on any price list in that harbor is better on the last page than on the first.**

### The four numbers and the nine figures a hand-over may get wrong, and Volume 09 gets right

**THE SECOND COLUMN'S BASE IS FOUR HUNDRED AND EIGHTY-NINE AT THE CLOSE OF FRIDAY THE THIRTEENTH OF AUGUST, being four hundred and thirty-nine plus fifty, and NOT three hundred and thirty-nine, which is the close of the fourteenth of July past. THE FOURTH COLUMN AT THE HOUR OF CHAPTER 400'S READING IS ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FOUR, not one hundred and four. THE FIGURE SHORT OF THE WAGE OF FOUR MARKS AT THE LAST PAGE IS FOUR HUNDRED AND EIGHTY PENCE, BEING THREE MARKS, and the bag is one hundred and sixty pence, being one mark. THE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIFTH LINE IS THE LAST LINE IN THAT LEDGER AND THE COLUMN IS NOT CLOSED, AND VOLUME 09 MAY NOT ENTER A HUNDRED AND TWENTY-SIXTH LINE IN THAT LEDGER. The forty-third wage Tuesday fell on Tuesday the seventeenth of August and the forty-fourth falls on Tuesday the twenty-fourth, which is the first day after this volume, and forty-three weeks stand fallen due with no envelope against any of them on the last page and nobody wrote one word under any of it saying anybody was going to pay it.**

**THE NINE FIGURES VOLUME 09 MUST NOT RE-DERIVE, EIGHT OF THEM COUNTED OFF THE FACE OF CHAPTER 400 AND THE NINTH RULED ON HERE: the notice on its wall for ninety-eight days; the bellwright not asked for one hundred days; the two objects of nobody's four hundred and thirty-eight days old; the bench under that pump bare for the two hundred and fourth night; **the two lights off the point — THE CHAPTERS' LAST FIGURE FOR THAT RUN IS NINETEEN DAYS, ON THE FACE OF CHAPTER 397, COUNTED FROM THE HOUR THEY WERE FIRST SEEN ON THE EVENING OF SUNDAY THE FIRST OF AUGUST PAST, AND THE TWENTY-TWO DAYS THAT A STATE FILE GIVES IS ON NO PAGE OF CHAPTER 400 AND IS NOT A FIGURE OF THE BOOK;** the ninety at seventy days with no seventy-first; the second seam fouled about a foot and seven inches on the weather side and nothing on the other, with its use closed at four figures and no fifth; the mole-head light out with its lens out since the seventh of May; and a bag of one mark against a wage of four.**

**AND THE FOUR THINGS A VOLUME 09 WRITER MAY NOT INHERIT AS A TASK: THE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-SIXTH LINE IN THAT LEDGER; A HUNDRED AND SEVENTY-FIRST DAY OF THE NINETY; A FORTY-FOURTH WAGE TUESDAY PAID; AND A SIXTEENTH LOSS OF FLOUR.**

### The relationship pressure at the end of Volume 08

- **Calder and Mara. THE APOLOGY REMAINS PAID AND UNFORGIVEN AND UNTHANKED, AND THE COMMITTED RELATIONSHIP HAS BEGUN, ONCE, ON THE CROWN OF THAT MOLE ON THE TWENTY-SECOND AT ABOUT SIX, IN A FEW SENTENCES.** It is not a marriage, the marriage is Volume 12's and is public, the work is not merged, she is not restored, and forty marks first after food is neither reduced nor paid at the last page. He is going to be told before and not after; she is not going to ask; if she does not like it that is what happens and she will not make a scene about it in the shed either. **She says that if either of them starts thanking the other for it she will stop coming up that hill, and it is not the apology and she says so herself, and she has the apology given on the water on the twenty-first of July and has not forgiven it then and has not forgiven it since and is not asking for a second one.** The yard has entered it in no column and is not going to, and nobody in that harbor is going to be told, and no word of it has been said twice.
- **Calder and Nessa. The pair the record stands on, and the last page of the volume is read by her and not by him.** She priced a day out loud before anybody agreed to it at every point where a day was agreed, wrote the master's own words and her own reason against them unjoined, put the fifth answer, which is a person, out of the first column, and on the last page read the four columns back in full in her own left hand and stated both definitions on the face of the reading. She put her hand on nothing, shut the leaf and put it under her own coat, and neither of them said one word about the figure it gave. On the last page of the volume she is the one who said the thing about the water, and it is about a mark fouled about a foot and seven inches and a ladder in another man's book that nobody has explained.
- **Calder and Alden. DO NOT MOVE, AND A VOLUME 09 MAY NOT MOVE HIM EITHER.** Occupied from ten until four on all fifty days, never approached, nothing on that bench read as a gift, one shoe beside him that is not his and that has been there since the third of May past, and neither brother went near the other at any hour of any of the fifty days. No fragment, no report talk, no second story, no confession. **The partial confession is Volume 09's and the original repair log is Volume 15's.**
- **Calder and Bevin. Unchanged and not in a room.** Off the stone since the fifteenth of May, forty marks whole, the three nots standing unasked for a sixth week, third column empty and unappointed on all fifty days with his hand at the head of it, the name beside it not said again, and his surname on no page of the fifty chapters.
- **Calder and Tobias Wren. Looked at, never asked, never thanked, never sent for, never a teacher, door or sacrifice; lock L27a holds.** On the crown of that mole from ten until four on all fifty days, sixty-one, eleven pieces of a boat behind him, a boat's hook in his right hand, and he is not the man on the far bench. **He says one sentence in the whole volume and it is on the face of Chapter 385, and nobody asks him which one and nobody says anything afterwards, and that is the correct use of him.**
- **Calder and the wardrobe.** Every man and woman the volume names is on a page, and **none of the above is a witness, a symbol, an officer, a member of anything or a courier.** Two are available to Volume 09: **ISAAC FELL, a caulker of about twenty-three, on a day and a wage and an hour and on nothing else, who told that yard he would not be on the stone on the Sunday and that the day he is not asked is the day there is not one; and SAUL DRURY, a copying clerk of the circuit office, about forty, named on a paper on a door as the one person who will be present in that room at the hour named, and whom nobody in that harbor has seen.**

SEVEN BOATS WENT OUT ON A BREACH OF THE FIRST CLAUSE ON A FLOOD AND CAME BACK ON THE SIXTH. AND STANDING WITH THOSE SIX: a page of six names on a mole with a boat as a price and no figure and a stone in one man's own pocket; a municipal claim on one of the three things in the circuit custody room that cannot be taken back without a request nobody in that harbor is going to make; a box in an office on the west basin that is no longer empty, and another box on the other paper that is and that a man of about fifty wants left empty; a municipal paper of the eighteenth of July naming two boats and three men and a tide with a door open four days up that coast and nobody at it; a slip of paper with a figure on it and no name on it in a drawer with a sheet in it, not looked at, not priced, not headed; and a nine-line sheet with a seal on it in the front street of that harbor since the fourteenth of August, which nobody there put up, which nobody has taken down, which nobody there has answered, which names no person and no harbor and puts no figure on it, and which is true enough on the face of it that nobody who reads it can go up the street and say it is a lie. NONE OF THE ABOVE IS PAID, ADVANCED, REDUCED OR IMPROVED ON ANY DAY OF THE FIFTY.**
